This vignette will showcase all of the basic functionality found in the `varkit` package.

## Setup

We start off by loading the package and defining the path to the VCF file we
wish to load. The file can be either compressed or uncompressed, but for this
example we will use a block-gzipped VCF.

```{r setup}
library(varkit)

# This might need to be increased for large VCFs
Sys.setenv("VROOM_CONNECTION_SIZE" = 1e6)

path <- system.file("extdata", "celegans.vcf.bgz", package = "varkit")
```

> NOTE: if you want to use `tidyverse` or more specifically `stringr`, it is
> recommended to load that library first.

## Loading a VCF into R

In it's simplest form you would load a VCF file into memory like so:

```{r read_simple, eval = FALSE}
vcf <- read_vcf(path, ploidy = 2)
```

However, it is good practice to first validate if the VCF header is parsed correctly:

```{r header}
header <- read_vcf_header(path)
print(header)
```

The most important information here is printed last (located under
`header$col_names`), the column names. If the VCF file is recognised correctly
it should list all of the fixed fields and samples present in your VCF.

If you want to exclude specific samples, or if you know you are not going to
use certain fixed fields and want to save memory, column names listed in the
header can be provided to the read vcf function in order to exclude them. 

For example here we exclude the INFO and FILTER fixed fields and the sample N2:


```{r read}
vcf <- read_vcf(path, ploidy = 2, skip_cols = c("info", "filter", "N2"))
print(vcf)
```

## Accessing specific fields

The `read_vcf()` function returns a special "varkit" object that holds all of
the information parsed from the VCF. This information should be accessed trough
designated functions, the most important of which are:

```{r access}
samples(vcf)

fixed(vcf)

geno(vcf)
```

> This syntax is similar to for example accessing the column names of a data
> frame `colnames(df)`.

## Getting help

Functions like `read_vcf()`, `read_vcf_header()`, and `geno()` return objects
with special classes, giving them access to an array of build in functions. To
check which functions are available for ANY given object use the `vakit_help()`
function:

```{r help}
varkit_help(vcf)
```

## Accessing header metadata

In this example header metadata can be accessed both from the `vcf` and `header`
objects, like so:

```{r metdata}
metadata <- meta(vcf)
print(metadata, verbose = FALSE)
```

However, you might notice that although the returned object is a data frame,
most of the information is stored in the `$value` column and cannot be easily
accessed. VarKit provides a function to parse these values, but this requires
you to select the type of field to be parsed. You can get an overview of the
available fields using:

```{r meta_summary}
summary(metadata)
```

Using this information we can then use the `parse_meta_type()` function to
parse the metadata of a specific type. For example we can lookup what the
different values in the INFO fields mean, or we can access the size of the
contigs:

```{r meta_parse}
parse_meta_type(vcf, "INFO")

parse_meta_type(vcf, "contig")
```

## Masking

A common operation when working with VCF is removing specific sites, based on
various criteria. In VarKit this is achieved trough the `mask()` function, which
either requires you to input a logical vector (TRUE if the site should be
masked) or a data frame with columns "chorm" and "pos" containing the sites to
be masked. For this example we will use a logical vector to mask/hide all sites on
chromosome I:

```{r mask}
# This is a logical vector
mask_site <- fixed(vcf)$chrom == "I"

# Be sure to reassign the returned object to `vcf` otherwise the mask will not take effect
vcf <- mask(vcf, site = mask_site)

# Use the summary function to check the number of visible sites
summary(vcf)
```

Now if we access data inside of the VCF the masked sites will no longer be
returned. For example if we retrieve the fixed fields we can see that the sites
with CHROM = "I" are missing (if you look back, you can see that they were
previously on top):

```{r mask_check}
fixed(vcf)
```

Masking can be performed multiple times in sequence:

```{r mask_seq}
# Let's use a data frame this time around
sites_to_mask <- dplyr::filter(fixed(vcf), qual < 1000)
vcf <- mask(vcf, site = sites_to_mask)
summary(vcf)
```

### Using multiple masks

This process is called 'masking' not 'removing', because the sites are not
actually removed from memory, they are just skipped by the VarKit functions.
This allows you to quickly unmask sites or restore an exported set of masked sites.

In this example we will fist export the mask we just created (which masks sites
on CHROM = "I" or sites with a QUAL < 1000) and assign it to the `my_mask`
variable, then we will remove the mask from the vcf object which can verify
trough the `summary()` function:

```{r mask_export}
my_mask <- export_mask(vcf)
vcf <- unmask_all(vcf)
summary(vcf)
```

If we later decide that we need the mask again, we can import it:

```{r mask_import}
vcf <- import_mask(vcf, my_mask)
summary(vcf)
```

In this way you could use different masks for different parts of your
analysis/script.

### Removing sites

In some cases, e.g. when you need to free memory or when you need maximum
retrieval speed, it is possible to entirely remove sites (meaning they cannot be
retrieved by unmasking):

```{r mask_remove}
reduced_vcf <- remove_masked(vcf)
summary(reduced_vcf)
```

## Writing VCF files

Varkit also has the ability to write VCF files. This is useful for example when
you have removed specific sites or samples and want to write the reduced file.

Moreover, masks are also stored in the FILTER column of the resulting VCF file
if `replace_filter = TRUE`, allowing you to save and load a masked VCF:

```{r mask_save}
temp_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".vcf.bz2")
write_vcf(vcf, path = temp_file, replace_filter = TRUE)

read_vcf(temp_file, ploidy = 2)
```

> NOTE: the `readr` library (which is used internally) does not support writing
> in the block-gzipped format that is expected by many other tools. To achieve
> this you can export to plain ".vcf" and convert the file using the "bcftools"
> CLI.

## Detecting linkage between sites

Lastly, the VarKit package provides functions to detect linkage between sites.
These functions use the `stats::cor(..., method = "pearson", use =
"pairwise.complete.obs")` internally, thus you can lookup its documentation for
more information.

In order for this to work `geno(vcf)` should contain only **numeric** values (or
NA). Most likely you genotype fields will be in the string format and thus need
to be converted. How to achieve this is highly circumstantial and will require
manual parsing/conversion. For tips take a look at the "Notes for advanced
users" section at the bottom.

As you might have noticed, the example file contains genotype calls (GT, e.g.
"0/1"), which will first convert to numeric dosages using a hidden function:

```{r convert_geno}
# The function below is not exported as it is not very robust, use it with caution!
vcf$geno <- varkit:::.bi_gt2dosage(vcf$geno)
```

Although you could use the `find_linked_sites()` function directly, one larger
VCF files you can speed up the process by first check for identical columns
(i.e. R^2 = 1):

```{r identical_sites, results = 'hide'}
llist <- find_identical_sites(vcf, cores = 1)
```

```{r identical_sites_summary}
summary(llist)
```

This will return a "link_list" object that tracks which sites (by their index)
are linked to each other and contains information on which sites to mask to
remove linkage (see also `varkit_help(llist)`). Thus, this object can then be
removed to mask sites (This will mask all but the centre most site out of sets
of identical/linked sites):

```{r mask_identical}
vcf <- mask(vcf, site = llist)
summary(vcf)
```

Now that identical sites are masked we can check for linkage on the reduced set
of sites. Here we will use an cutoff of R^2 = 0.7:

```{r linked_sites, results = 'hide'}
llist <- find_linked_sites(vcf, cutoff = 0.7, cores = 1)
vcf <- mask(vcf, site = llist)
```

```{r linked_sites_summary}
summary(vcf)
```

It is important to know that `find_indentical_sites()` checks entire
chromosomes/scaffolds, whereas `find_linked_sites()` only checks for linkage
within a specified window (by default this is 50,000 bp). To check entire
chromosomes in the latter case set the "window" option to 0 or -1.

> Both of these function support multi-threading trough the "cores" option and
> only look for identical/linked columns within chromosomes/scaffolds. This
> latter can be disabled trough the "by_chrom" option, but this will greatly
> increase computational load.

### Reading/writing link_list objects to file

It might be interesting to store the information about linked sites to consult
later on:

```{r llist_wirte}
temp_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
write_link_list(llist, path = temp_file)
```

Which can then be read back into memory like so:

```{r llist_read}
llist2 <- read_link_list(temp_file)
summary(llist2)
```

## Notes for advanced users

It is safe to directly modify the varkit object using the `$` operator as long
as `nrow(vcf$fixed) == ncol(vcf$geno) == length(vcf$use_sites)`, the
`vcf$fixed$chrom` & `vcf$fixed$pos` columns are retained, and `vcf$geno` keeps
the 'varkit_geno' class (the latter may be violated when extracting, e.g.
`geno(vcf)[, 1]`, which will remove the class).

The attentive reader might have noticed that we have already made use of this before:

```{r advanced_example, eval = FALSE}
vcf$geno <- varkit:::.bi_gt2dosage(vcf$geno)
```

To retain the "varkit_geno" class use the `varkit_geno()` function, e.g.:

```{r advanced_geno, eval = FALSE}
vcf$geno <- varkit_geno(my_matrix)
```
